Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 18
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Police Officer
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Discomfort: Feeling uncomfortable, Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously, Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Vignette:
At eighteen, Kofi found himself grappling with memories that felt more like a heavy shroud than a distant past. Raised in a neighborhood where the echoes of domestic violence rang through thin walls, he had witnessed his mother being beaten by his father. The images from those nights were sharp and unforgiving: the sound of fists hitting flesh, the helpless cries, the panic that gripped his small body as he hid under his bed, trying to drown out the chaos. Even now, years later, Kofi could remember those moments vividly. The snapshots clung to him like a persistent shadow, each frame seared into his mind, replaying in an endless loop. 

As he moved into adulthood, Kofi chose to become a police officer, perhaps in an attempt to control the chaos he had once felt so powerless against. Yet, the weight of his childhood trauma followed him into this new role, shaping his perceptions and reactions in ways he couldn’t fully articulate. Each day on the job, he encountered situations that would trigger memories he sought to forget. The discomfort that washed over him in the presence of suspicious individuals, the way his heart raced as he noticed a potential weapon on a belt or in a pocket—these were constant reminders of the danger he had once experienced. He often found himself scanning for threats, a habit that had become second nature. Kofi had come to believe that he needed to be hyper-vigilant, that the world was filled with dangers he must assess at all times, especially in unfamiliar places. 

In the quiet moments of his life, Kofi often felt an eerie sense of foreboding. Silence, which others might find peaceful, settled heavily on his chest, filling him with dread that something terrible was about to unfold. He noticed how his body reacted when memories surfaced; he would feel the same tension, the same helplessness he felt as a child, as though he were once again curled up under his bed, trapped in a moment he could not escape. When he recalled the violence of his childhood, overwhelming grief washed over him, a reminder of the trauma he had not fully processed. 

Kofi’s relationships began to suffer as he became more withdrawn, isolating himself from friends and family. He couldn’t shake the feeling that he couldn’t rely on himself, that his reactions—his intense fear of being touched unexpectedly, the way he flinched at a friendly pat on the back—were signs that he was losing control. He often found himself avoiding social gatherings, fearing the unpredictability of unfamiliar faces and environments. This avoidance extended to his work as well; he would sometimes hesitate before entering a new neighborhood or stepping into a crowd, his mind racing with thoughts of what could go wrong. 

As time passed, Kofi’s symptoms intensified. The nightmares began, nightmares that brought back the vivid scenes of his childhood, where he could feel the blows, hear the screams, and taste the fear that had once gripped him so tightly. It was as if he was trapped in a cycle of grief and fear, convinced that he was teetering on the edge of madness. He often wondered if he was going crazy, grappling with the belief that his reactions were not normal, that he was somehow broken.

His decision to seek help came after a particularly difficult shift, during which he found himself frozen in the face of a domestic disturbance. He had been reminded of his own childhood, the sense of powerlessness overwhelming him. For the first time, he realized that he couldn’t carry this burden alone anymore. What frightened Kofi most was the thought that he might continue to experience life through this lens of fear, unable to escape the memories that haunted him. As he sat in the therapist's office, he hoped for understanding, for a way to reclaim his sense of self and the confidence he had lost along the way. The journey ahead felt daunting, but for the first time in years, Kofi held onto a flicker of hope that healing was possible.
